proof:
# Facet-free maximizers form an empty lattice polytope

Assume d>=2 and positive mixed d-volume. Let C be a compact convex
body and mu its measure on the positive integer fibers K_z, z in P.
Suppose every supporting hyperplane of every K_z has zero
H_(d-1)-measure. Write M=mu(S), D(y)=inf_(closed H containing y)mu(H)/M,
and beta=max_(y in S)D(y)>0. All maxima exist by upper
semicontinuity and compactness; positivity follows, for example, from
the already proved mixed Helly centerpoint bound. This note uses no OC
bound.

Let T be the set of points of S attaining beta. The conclusions are:

1. Every nonvertical minimizing through-point cap at a point of T
   strictly excludes every other point of T.
2. Projection is one-to-one on T. Its image Q is in convex position,
   conv(Q) intersect Z^n=Q, and |Q|<=2^n.
3. With continuous normal of length one, all such minimizing caps
   at each fixed y_i in T have a uniform negative margin at each
   other y_j in T. In particular they miss one fixed continuous
   ball about y_j in its own fiber.
4. Every minimal balanced active circuit at y_i gives a linear
   functional on the integer coordinates strictly exposing its base
   among the other maximizing bases.

The cardinality and exposed-point statements are structural. No lower
bound beta>=2^(-n)gamma_d is inferred from them.

## 1. No common minimizing cap

Positive-depth points lie in the interiors of their positive fibers,
and depth is attained by a nonvertical through-point cap. Complete
proofs, including finite-tilt saturation and the boundary-fiber issue,
are recorded in `candidate b989614dc4f86228` and
`candidate f2d1fbdd5a877f5b`.

Fix distinct y_i,y_j in T and a minimizing cap H={L>=0} through y_i,
with unit continuous normal. Its mass is beta M. If L(y_j)>0, move
its boundary parallel through y_j. The resulting cap still contains
y_j and loses a positive slab in the interior of K_(base y_j), so
it has mass less than beta M, a contradiction.

If L(y_j)=0, the same cap minimizes at both points. Choose any
ambient affine h with h(y_i)=0 and h(y_j)=1. The proved ambient
facet-flux inequality gives

    A <= sum_supporting integral dist(h,[0,1]) dH_(d-1),

where A is the total proper-section measure. The right side is zero
under the facet-null assumption, whereas the two endpoint fibers
give A>0 (one fiber suffices if the bases agree). This is impossible.
Thus L(y_j)<0. This proof does not require an integer intermediate
point on the segment between y_i and y_j.

## 2. Integer convex combinations of maxima

For any finite points y_1,...,y_k in T and positive weights t_i of
sum one, their combination y lies in C. If its base is integer, then
y belongs to S and has depth at least beta: every halfspace containing
y contains at least one y_i, since its affine margin at y is their
weighted average. Hence y belongs to T.

Let H={L>=0} attain depth at y and have L(y)=0. If any y_i differs
from y, Section 1 gives L(y_i)<0; those equal to y have zero margin.
But then sum t_i L(y_i)<0, contrary to L(y)=0. Thus ALL positively
weighted points in this integer-base combination must coincide.

Two distinct maxima in the same fiber would have a nontrivial
midpoint of integer base, which is now impossible. Projection is
therefore injective. If two distinct maximizing bases shared parity,
their midpoint would be integer and again impossible. Consequently
T is finite with at most 2^n points; put Q=projection(T).

For any z in conv(Q) intersect Z^n, use a convex representation by
Q and the corresponding points of T. The preceding argument says
that representation has just one distinct positively weighted point,
so z is a member of Q. It also says no point of Q is a convex
combination of the others. This proves both empty lattice hull and
convex position. In fact the integer sections of conv(T) consist
exactly of the original singleton maximizing fibers.

## 3. Uniform separation, including unbounded integer tilts

Fix distinct maxima y_i=(p_i,x_i), y_j=(p_j,x_j). Write a minimizing
cap at y_i as

    L(z,x)=a.(z-p_i)+u.(x-x_i),   |u|=1.

All its margins at y_j are negative by Section 1. Suppose they have
supremum zero. Choose such caps with L_k(y_j)->0 and u_k->u along a
subsequence. Because P is finite, pass to extended-real limits of
every a_k.(z-p_i). Let I be the finite-limit indices, and let E be
the span of their base differences. Their evaluations specify a
limiting linear functional ell on E. The replacement

    a'_k=a_k-P_E a_k+ell

has exactly the limiting evaluations on I and unchanged divergence
signs on the other indices. For one sufficiently large k, using u
instead of u_k, every divergent fiber is fully saturated with the
correct sign. This gives a finite normal a' whose cap has the exact
limiting mass. On finite-limit fibers, convergence of cap volumes
uses only that a nonzero continuous normal has zero d-volume on its
boundary. On divergent fibers convergence is uniform full/empty.

In particular j belongs to I: its original evaluations converge to
-u.(x_j-x_i). The resulting cap therefore passes through both
y_i and y_j and has mass beta M. This contradicts Section 1.
There is consequently a number delta_ij>0 such that every minimizing
cap at y_i satisfies L(y_j)<=-delta_ij.

Since |u|=1, all these caps exclude the continuous ball of radius
delta_ij/2 centered at x_j. Decrease the radius further if needed
to put that ball inside K_(p_j). Finiteness of T permits a common
positive separation radius over all ordered distinct pairs when
|T|>=2. No assertion is made about a uniform bound over different
bodies or along a limiting sequence.

## 4. Base exposure from each active circuit

At a maximum y_i, active projected continuous normals have zero in
their convex hull; the compactness and own-fiber slab proof is given
in `unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`.
Take any actual positive balanced circuit

    L_k(z,x)=a_k.(z-p_i)+u_k.(x-x_i),
    lambda_k>0, sum lambda_k=1, sum lambda_k u_k=0.

Set b_i=sum lambda_k a_k. At a different maximizing point y_j,
Section 1 gives

    b_i.(p_j-p_i)=sum lambda_k L_k(y_j)<0.

Thus b_i exposes p_i strictly among the other maximizing bases.
For a singleton T the conclusion is vacuous; otherwise b_i cannot
vanish. The argument tracks the full integer coefficients and uses
actual minimizing caps, including all oblique orientations.

## Scope

Combined with outer strict-convex approximation, this describes
maximizers of arbitrarily accurate approximants to any full-volume
instance. Several maximizing points may merge, appear, or disappear
in a limit, and no parity bound is transferred to arbitrary faceted
fibers by that limit alone. Neither the finite set Q nor its exposing
circuits allocate the total mixed mass among at most 2^n convex
continuous sources. That quantitative step remains unproved.
